title: Looking back: year four
hook: the schools, each in its own words
tomorrow: why does a sutta open with 'thus have I heard'?

segments.voice: Yesterday, year three: the great story, carried by a beginner's one verse. Today, year four, when the story split into schools.

Every flight safety talk says it: put on your own mask first, then help the person next to you. Some people hear that as selfish. Others hear it as the only way anyone gets helped. Buddhists have their own long version of that argument, and year four heard it from both sides. Free yourself first, or vow to stay until everyone is free? Two ideals, the arahant and the bodhisattva, and each school says it in its own words.
screen: `YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.` → `SELFISH, OR THE ONLY WAY?` → `THE ARAHANT. THE BODHISATTVA.`

segments.voice: First voice, the Theravada, the school of the elders. Its ideal is the arahant, one who has finished the journey, free of grief and every fetter, as the Dhammapada puts it. Its best case comes from a sutta: someone sunk in the mud can't pull another out. Someone who isn't sunk can. Get free, and your help becomes real. And the arahants in the suttas don't vanish; the Buddha sends his first ones out to wander for the welfare of the many. Second voice, the Mahayana, the great vehicle, the school of Mai's family's chùa. Its ideal is the bodhisattva, who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings. The Diamond Sutra has the vow: however many beings there are, I will lead them all to nirvana. Shantideva, a teacher in that tradition, asks to remain as long as space remains and beings suffer, to ease their pain. Its best case: a freedom that leaves anyone behind isn't finished yet. Both voices are about compassion. They differ on the shape of the road. And each keeps a place for the other's ideal: Mahayana temples honor the arahants, and the Theravada tells the Buddha's own past lives, in the Jataka stories, as a bodhisatta on the long road. Year four didn't pick a winner. It opened many doors, and walked through each.
screen: `THERAVADA: THE ARAHANT.` · `NO ONE SUNK IN MUD PULLS ANOTHER OUT.` · `MAHAYANA: THE BODHISATTVA VOW.` · `A FREEDOM FOR ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `MANY DOORS.`

segments.voice: Bring your palms together at your chest, the gesture called anjali, used in temples of every school you met this year. Hold it, and on each breath out, silently name one gift a school gave you: a way of sitting, a chant, a story, a question. If one gift keeps coming back, stay with it.
Looking back, at year four: the schools, each in its own words, two ideals of one compassion.
Keep this one: many doors, one teacher behind them. Day four of the summit, done.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhism is practiced in places such as Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos; Mahayana in places such as Vietnam, China, Korea and Japan; many temples of both welcome people from the other.

options: same Buddha, different schools: one stresses getting free, one vows to free all. many doors.

chat.meaning: Theravada holds up the arahant who has finished the journey; Mahayana, the bodhisattva who vows to free all beings. Both teach compassion; neither has to be wrong.

tie.story: The Theravada says the sunk can't pull out the sunk; the Mahayana bodhisattva vows to lead all beings to nirvana.

Theravada.meaning: the school of the elders; its ideal is the arahant

arahant.meaning: one who has finished the journey, freed

Mahayana.meaning: the great vehicle; its ideal is the bodhisattva

bodhisattva.meaning: one who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings

Shantideva.meaning: a Mahayana teacher who wrote on the bodhisattva way

anjali.meaning: palms together at the chest, a gesture of respect

sources.ref: Dhammapada 90 (the one who has finished the journey), Arahant chapter
Majjhima Nikaya 8 (Sallekha Sutta: one sunk in the mud cannot pull out another)
Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.11 (the first monks sent out for the welfare of the many)
Diamond Sutra (Vajracchedika), section 3 (the vow to lead all beings to nirvana)
Shantideva, Bodhicaryavatara 10.55 (as long as space remains)

notes: All five sources paraphrased. Dhp 90: no fever for one who has finished the journey, is free of grief, freed on all sides, with every fetter cast off. MN 8: it is impossible for one sunk in the mud to pull out another sunk in the mud. Mahavagga 1.11: 'walk, monks, on tour for the blessing of the many'. Diamond Sutra 3: however many beings, all are to be led to nirvana (the sutra then adds that no being is led; left out for brevity). Bodhicaryavatara 10.55. Confirm each.

Framing check: both ideals presented as compassion, neither ranked; the myth item and the chat's wrong reply name the popular 'original vs later extras' ranking as the misreading. Confirm the Theravada and Mahayana framing is fair to both.
Vietnamese Buddhism as largely Mahayana (Thiền and Pure Land) is standard; Mai's family's chùa is Mahayana in the cast. howItsDone lists countries only as examples. Confirm.

Each school keeping a place for the other's ideal: arahants (luohan) honored in Chinese/Vietnamese Mahayana temples; the Jataka tells the Buddha's past lives as the Bodhisatta in Theravada. Confirm wording.
Anjali as a gesture used across schools: standard. Confirm wording 'temples of every school you met this year' (kept to the path's own schools).

Shape: debate (two ideals inside the tradition, each given its best case; the fork asks for the Theravada steelman). Mai's storyline: Ava's cousin's photos of Thai monks; Ava asks if one of them is doing it wrong.
Surprising fact: the Theravada's own sutta image: one sunk in mud cannot pull out another.
